title: What can you say about vitamin C in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 8 wordings for vitamin C; the strongest is "Provides an antioxidant that helps protect cells against damage from free radicals" (strong, 6-2,000 mg a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Prevents, cures or shortens colds and flu".

supported_wordings.wording: Provides an antioxidant that helps protect cells against damage from free radicals.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists antioxidant wording, and the EU authorizes protection of cells from oxidative stress after EFSA review.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Health Canada: 6-2,000 mg a day for adults 19 and older (6-1,800 mg at 14 to 18). EU: at least 12 mg, 15% of the 80 mg EU reference value (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Annex XIII). ODS upper limit: 2,000 mg a day for adults.
supported_wordings.form: Ascorbic acid or a listed ascorbate, counted as vitamin C

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Prevents, cures or shortens colds and flu
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names infectious diseases; the supported wording is normal immune function.
Implies an effect on infections; the supported wording is normal immune function.
Names a disease. FDA's qualified claims on antioxidant vitamins and cancer come with disclaimers saying the evidence is limited or highly uncertain (see fda_health_claims).
Promises to heal damage to the body. Health Canada's wound-healing use is a Canada only note.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition
